text_post: The answer is "d) 60°" First you divide the circle of 360° by 12 to get 30°, which is the interior angle of each triangle created by the flat side and the center of the coin. Then subtract 30° from 180° and divide by 2 to get the other angles of the triangle, which is 75°. Double that to get the interior angle of each corner of the coin, for 150°. Subtract that from the 180° straight line created by the touching faces of the coins for 30° from vertical, and double it again to get the angle between the adjacent faces, or 60°. What we would call 9th grade Geometry around here.

text_post: That's not it at all.  You make it sound like childish answers such as these come from a magical fairy dust ability of children that we should mourn as lost in adults, but instead it comes from ignorance. Adults have actual experience with the size of freezers as we use them every week, if not every day.  Most adults have shopped for one, and know approximately how big a normal household freezer is.  Adults also know the approximate size of an elephant, having seen one on TV next to scale-providing objects such as other humans on or next to said elephant, or having seen one several times in a zoo. Kids on the other hand, depending on their age, likely have ZERO experience with freezers as their parents will do all the shopping, putting away groceries, and cooking.  At best its an ephemeral object in the back of their mind with no true dimension that they have likely never actually seen the inside of (too short to see in).  Similarly, an elephant is a magical creature usually seen as small stickers or images in books.  Add to this a young child's underdeveloped sense of size comparison and other necessary experiences and you end up with the childish answer. Most adults would give a similar answer if you asked them "how do you put a zergox into a belarusbox?"
